examGuide.title: Mental model and derivation
examGuide.body:
Reflexivity checks diagonal pairs, symmetry checks reversed pairs, and transitivity checks composed paths. Antisymmetry allows mutual relation only between equal elements; it is not the negation of symmetry. Equivalence relations partition the domain. A transitive closure must include paths discovered through newly added pairs, so one pass through the initial edges need not suffice.

**Key relationship:** a ~ b ⇔ a mod m = b mod m gives m residue classes on the integers

examGuide.title: A repeatable solving procedure
examGuide.body:
1. Check each property independently.
2. Exhibit a missing required pair.
3. Iterate closure to a fixed point.

examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: For relation-property questions, apply the definition to every relevant tuple rather than inferring a property from a few pairs. An equivalence relation partitions its set into disjoint nonempty classes. Two elements are related precisely when their classes agree. A function constant on each class induces a well-defined quotient map; injectivity of that map requires different classes to have different images.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
An equivalence relation on a 7-element set has classes of sizes 2,2,3. How many ordered pairs belong to the relation?

**Answer: 17.** Within a class of size k, every element is related to all k members, including itself, giving k² ordered pairs. Across classes there are none. Count=2²+2²+3²=17.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
A symmetric relation may contain both (x,y) and (y,x). Antisymmetry allows both only when x=y; it is not the negation of symmetry.

Antisymmetry does not mean “not symmetric”; equality is both symmetric and antisymmetric.

examGuide.title: Worked question patterns
examGuide.body:
#### Pattern 1 · MCQ

R={(1,1),(2,2),(1,2)} on {1,2} is:

- **A.** Symmetric
- **B.** Not reflexive
- **C.** An equivalence relation
- **D.** A partial order

**Answer: D.** It is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. It is not symmetric because (2,1) is missing.

#### Pattern 2 · MSQ

Select true statements.

- **A.** Equivalence relations are reflexive
- **B.** Symmetry implies transitivity
- **C.** Every symmetric relation is antisymmetric
- **D.** Equivalence classes partition the domain

**Answer: A, D.** Equivalence implies reflexivity and partitions the domain. A symmetric relation with both (1,2) and (2,1) is not antisymmetric; symmetry alone does not imply transitivity.

#### Pattern 3 · NAT

How many reflexive relations exist on a three-element set?



**Answer: 64.** Three diagonal pairs are mandatory. Six off-diagonal pairs are optional independently: 2⁶=64.

examGuide.title: Work through the supplied PYQs
examGuide.body:
#### GATE 2023 CS · Q49 · MSQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/relations?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Relations and equivalence classes. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. If x and x′ represent the same equivalence class, f(x)=f(x′), so F([x]) is independent of the chosen representative. A is false.
2. For any b∈B, surjectivity of f gives x with f(x)=b, so F is onto. If F([x])=F([y]), then f(x)=f(y), which means [x]=[y]; hence F is injective.
3. Both properties make F bijective. Select **B,C,D**.

#### GATE 2026 CS2 · Q26 · MSQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/relations?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Relations and equivalence classes. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. xRx because x² is a square; xy=yx gives symmetry.
2. Assign every integer its squarefree part. A product xy is square exactly when x and y have the same squarefree part. Equality of this part is transitive, proving C.
3. Antisymmetry fails: 1R4 and 4R1 but 1≠4. Select **A,B,C**.
